title: Lecture #32: Java List Interface Deep Dive

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of the `List` interface as described in the lecture?
options: Every element has a position (index)
Insertion order is preserved
Duplicate elements are silently dropped
Elements can be accessed by index
questions.explanation: A List keeps elements in a positional, insertion-ordered sequence, allows duplicates and supports index access such as `get(i)`. Rejecting duplicates is the defining property of a Set, not a List. Adding the same value twice to an ArrayList stores it twice.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `set(1, 5)` replaces the element at index 1, giving [1, 5, 3] (size unchanged). `add(0, 9)` inserts at index 0 and shifts the rest right, giving [9, 1, 5, 3], so `get(1)` is 1. The common mistake is treating `set` like an insert or `add(index, e)` like a replace.

questions.question: You are writing new code that needs a LIFO stack (e.g. for undo history). A teammate suggests `java.util.Stack`. What does the lecture recommend instead?
options: `Vector`, because it is the modern replacement for Stack
`HashTable`, because it gives O(1) push and pop
`LinkedList` accessed only via `get(0)` and `set(0, x)`
`ArrayDeque`, which can act as both a queue and a stack
questions.explanation: `Vector`, `Stack` and `Hashtable` are legacy classes; `Stack` is just an array-based stack built on Vector. The lecture points to `ArrayDeque` as the modern class that can be used as both a Queue and a Stack. Vector is not a replacement — it is the legacy dynamic array that Stack itself extends.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
options: It prints `[1, 2, 3, 7]`, because `copyOf` returns a fresh modifiable list
It throws `UnsupportedOperationException` at `l2.add(7)`
It does not compile, because `List.copyOf` returns an array
It prints `[1, 2, 3]`, because the add is silently ignored
questions.explanation: `List.of(...)` and `List.copyOf(...)` both return unmodifiable lists, so any structural change such as `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` at runtime. The code compiles because the static type is still `List<Integer>`, which declares `add`. To get a modifiable copy you would use `new ArrayList<>(l)`.

questions.question: Using the lecture's growth rule `newCapacity = oldCapacity + oldCapacity / 2`, an ArrayList's backing array starts at capacity 4. What is its capacity after it has had to grow twice?
questions.explanation: The first growth gives 4 + 4/2 = 6 and the second gives 6 + 6/2 = 9, i.e. about 1.5× each time (the lecture's 4 → 6 → 9). 8 and 16 come from assuming the array doubles, which is how many people describe it but is not ArrayList's rule. Each growth allocates a new array and copies the old elements across.

questions.question: You will load about 1,000,000 records into an `ArrayList` and afterwards the list will never grow; memory is tight. Which plan uses ArrayList's capacity features correctly?
options: Create `new ArrayList<>(1_000_000)`; it then already holds 1,000,000 null slots, so you can fill it with `set(i, record)`
Declare it as `List<Record> l` and call `l.ensureCapacity(1_000_000)` and later `l.trimToSize()`
Pre-size it with `new ArrayList<>(1_000_000)` (or `ensureCapacity`) to avoid repeated grow-and-copy, then call `trimToSize()` after loading to drop unused capacity
Nothing can be done; ArrayList always starts at capacity 10 and grows by 1.5×
questions.explanation: Capacity is the length of the backing array, size is the number of elements; pre-sizing avoids many resize copies, and `trimToSize()` shrinks capacity to the current size. A capacity constructor does not create elements — size is still 0, so `set(i, ...)` would throw `IndexOutOfBoundsException`. Also, `ensureCapacity` and `trimToSize` are declared on `ArrayList`, not on `List`, so calling them through a `List` reference does not compile.

questions.question: Java's `LinkedList` is a doubly linked list with `first` and `last` references. For a LinkedList of size 10, how does `list.get(7)` locate the element?
options: It computes the memory address directly from the index, in O(1)
It always walks forward from `first`, visiting 7 links
It copies the nodes into an array and indexes into that array
Because 7 is not less than size/2, it starts at `last` and walks backward through `prev` links
questions.explanation: Each node has `next` and `prev`; LinkedList checks `index < size / 2` and starts from `first` for the front half, otherwise from `last` going backward — here 9 → 8 → 7. This halves the walk but access is still O(n), unlike ArrayList's O(1) random access. Nodes are scattered in memory, so no address can be computed from the index.

questions.question: What does this print (adapted from the lecture's Demo)?
options: Nothing — `listIterator(3)` throws IndexOutOfBoundsException because index 3 does not exist
questions.explanation: `listIterator(3)` places the cursor after the last element (an index equal to `size()` is allowed). `previousIndex()` reports the index of the element that `previous()` would return — 2, then 1, then 0 — and `previous()` moves the cursor back each time until `hasPrevious()` is false. Unlike a plain Iterator, a ListIterator can move in both directions and start at any position.

questions.question: On Java 21, you want one helper method that accepts either an `ArrayList` or an `ArrayDeque` and returns its last element without index arithmetic. Which declaration works for both?
options: `static <E> E last(SequencedCollection<E> c) { return c.getLast(); }`
`static <E> E last(Collection<E> c) { return c.getLast(); }`
`static <E> E last(List<E> c) { return c.get(c.size() - 1); }`
`static <E> E last(Iterable<E> c) { return c.getLast(); }`
questions.explanation: Java 21's `SequencedCollection` sits between `Collection` and `List`/`Deque` and declares `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `addLast`, `removeFirst` and `removeLast`, so both ArrayList and ArrayDeque can be passed. `Collection` and `Iterable` have no `getLast()`, so those versions do not compile. The `List` version compiles but rejects an ArrayDeque, which is not a List.

questions.question: After the `addAll` and `remove` calls, what do the three index lookups print?
questions.explanation: `addAll(1, ...)` inserts the three elements starting at index 1: [1, 2, 9, 2, 2, 3]. `remove(Integer.valueOf(2))` calls `remove(Object)` and removes only the first 2: [1, 9, 2, 2, 3]. So `indexOf(2)` is 2, `lastIndexOf(2)` is 3, and `indexOf(5)` returns -1 because 5 is absent (not 0).
